title: When groups and totals disagree
note: Blind content review: canonical answer indices, explanations and transfer prompts intentionally withheld until independent choices and reasons are recorded.

items.prompt: In a fictional puzzle log, option A records 42 successes in 70 newcomer attempts and 18 successes in 20 experienced-player attempts. Which fraction gives A's success rate among newcomers?
Option A has 42 successes in 70 newcomer attempts and 18 in 20 experienced-player attempts. What is its success rate over all 90 recorded attempts?
options: 75 / 100, exactly 75%
42 / 70, exactly 60%
18 / 20, exactly 90%

items.prompt: A's pooled rate is exactly 2/3. B's pooled rate is 77/100. By approximately how many percentage points is B higher?
options: 15.50 percentage points
10.33 percentage points
0.1033 percentage points
77.00 percentage points

items.prompt: A has newcomer rate 60% (42/70) and experienced-player rate 90% (18/20). B has newcomer rate 50% (5/10) and experienced-player rate 80% (72/90). Which group-composition statement explains how B can have the higher pooled rate?
options: A gives greater weight to experienced players, its higher-rate group.
Each pooled rate gives equal weight to the two observed groups.
Both pooled rates use only the larger of the two group denominators.
B gives greater weight to experienced players, its higher-rate group.

items.prompt: The same fictional logs give A versus B rates of 60% versus 50% among newcomers, 90% versus 80% among experienced players, and about 66.67% versus 77% when pooled. Which statement is supported by those recorded counts?
options: A has a higher rate in both groups; B has a higher pooled rate.
B has a higher rate in both groups; A has a higher pooled rate.
Choosing A causes every player's chance of success to increase.
At least one of the six descriptive rates is arithmetically impossible.

items.prompt: In another fictional sample, newcomer rates are A: 8/10 and B: 6/10. Experienced-player rates are A: 4/10 and B: 9/10. Does this show the strict pattern of both within-group comparisons reversing when pooled?
options: Yes, because B has the higher rate after the counts are pooled.
No, because the two within-group comparisons point opposite ways.
No, because equally sized groups can never have different rates.
Yes, because any difference between group rates is a reversal.

items.prompt: Keep the first sample's group rates fixed: newcomers A 60%, B 50%; experienced players A 90%, B 80%. What are the reference rates if both options use a 50% newcomer / 50% experienced mix?
options: A about 66.67%; B 77%

items.prompt: A's newcomer rate is 60% and experienced-player rate is 90%. Apply a reference mix of 20% newcomers and 80% experienced players. What reference rate results?

A has no recorded newcomer attempts (0 successes out of 0) and 9 successes in 10 experienced-player attempts. What can the explorer report for A at a reference mix of 50% newcomers and 50% experienced players?
options: Unavailable: one positive-weight group has no observed rate.
45%: treat unobserved newcomers as having zero successes.
90%: apply the observed experienced rate to both groups.
100%: remove the empty group from every denominator.

items.prompt: A still has 0/0 newcomer attempts and 9/10 experienced-player attempts. Now the reference mix contains 0% newcomers and 100% experienced players. What reference rate can be computed without filling in a missing rate?
options: Unavailable at every reference mix

items.prompt: The puzzle counts come from observational logs, with no stated assignment procedure. To investigate whether switching a player from B to A would improve success, which next step addresses the missing causal information?
options: Pool all attempts and choose the option with the greater fraction.
Split on every recorded variable and choose the strongest subgroup.
Specify the intervention and examine assignment, timing and common causes.
Force a fifty-fifty group mix and treat its difference as the effect.

items.prompt: Suppose the chosen method can change whether a player completes optional practice, and practice can affect final puzzle success. The question concerns the method's total effect, including that practice pathway. Should comparing only within post-method practice groups automatically answer it?
options: Yes; removing any group difference always isolates total effects.
Yes; equal reference weights make post-method grouping harmless.
No; every pooled association already equals an intervention effect.
No; such grouping can remove part of the pathway being studied.
